title: Response to application from respondent United States

No. 26A446 
In the Supreme Court of the United States 
───────────
KYLE WAGNER, APPLICANT
v. 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
───────────
RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO THE APPLICATION 
FOR A STAY OF THE JUDGMENT OF THE UNITED STATES 
COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT 
───────────
D. JOHN SAUER
 Solicitor General 
 Counsel of Record 
 Department of Justice 
 Washington, D.C. 20530-0001 
 SupremeCtBriefs@usdoj.gov 
 (202) 514-2217

ii 
RELATED PROCEEDINGS 
United States District Court (E.D. Mich.): 
United States v. Wagner, No. 26-cr-20059 (Mar. 25, 2026) 
United States Court of Appeals (6th Cir.): 
United States v. Wagner, No. 26-1294 (Aug. 12, 2026)

(1) 
In the Supreme Court of the United States 
───────────
No. 26A446 
KYLE WAGNER, APPLICANT
v. 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
───────────
RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO THE APPLICATION 
FOR A STAY OF THE JUDGMENT OF THE UNITED STATES 
COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT 
───────────
The Solicitor General respectfully files this response to the application for a 
stay of the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit pending the disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari. Applicant, a promoter of antigovernment violence who has been charged with federal cyberstalking and threat offenses, seeks emergency relief based on his own willingness to prolong his pretrial 
proceedings—and thus his detention—in order to obtain rushed consideration of a 
standard-of-review issue on which he asserts a four-decade-old circuit disagreement, 
which this Court has declined to address before, and which has little apparent practical importance to his case or others. That is not an emergency, and relief should be 
denied. 
Applicant is a self-identified member of Antifa based in Minneapolis, Minnesota. After the Department of Homeland Security began an immigration-enforcement operation in the Twin Cities area last winter, applicant engaged in escalating 
attacks via social media against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and 
its perceived supporters—urging his followers to kill ICE agents and march on a fed-

2 
eral building with firearms, among other measures. To take one of the milder examples, which applicant now portrays as referring to “nonviolence or self-defense,” applicant urged his followers to “‘[g]o take [ICE agents’] f------ masks off and take their 
f------ guns.’” Appl. 7-8 (quoting Pet. App. 170a).1 Applicant also solicited funds to 
help him “evade detection by the authorities” and held himself out in a text-message 
exchange as able to assist with a plot to murder “a former high-ranking government 
official.” Pet. App. 2a, 5a. His campaign culminated in his “doxx[ing]” of a “pro-ICE” 
individual by revealing that individual’s personal information—including his and his 
parents’ addresses—on the Internet. Id. at 5a (citation omitted). When he was arrested on charges of violating federal laws prohibiting cyberstalking and transmitting 
threats, see 18 U.S.C. 875(c), 2261A(2), applicant pushed and spat on the arresting 
agents and, in his booking photo, made an obscene gesture that he clarified was “for 
the judge,” Pet. App. 6a (citation omitted). 
A magistrate judge ordered applicant detained pending trial in light of his lack 
of a stable job or housing and his desire to evade law enforcement. See 18 U.S.C. 
3142(e)(1) (mandating pretrial detention when “no condition or combination of conditions [of release] will reasonably assure the appearance of the person as required and 
the safety of any other person and the community”). But the district court, despite 
acknowledging the government’s “very strong argument” that applicant’s release 
would threaten the public safety, Pet. App. 143a, revoked applicant’s detention and 
ordered him released on conditions that would allow him to use the Internet and leave 
his residence (which could enable him to use the Internet unmonitored) for various 
purposes. The court of appeals reversed, recognizing that, given applicant’s evident 
1 Citations of “Pet. App.” herein refer to the appendix to applicant’s petition 
for a writ of certiorari, which was filed on September 18, 2026 (No. 26-391). Citations 
of “Appl. App.” refer to the appendix to applicant’s stay application.

3 
dangerousness and the inadequacy of the district court’s release conditions to protect 
the public, the correct result under the Bail Reform Act was that he be detained pending trial. In this Court, applicant seeks a stay of the court of appeals’ judgment pending the disposition of his recently filed petition for certiorari. 
Applicant satisfies none of the requirements for obtaining a stay from this 
Court. The Court is not likely to grant certiorari in this case. Although applicant 
asserts a decades-old circuit conflict over the appellate standard of review for bail 
decisions, the Court has previously declined to review the same purported conflict, 
see Gray v. United States, 143 S. Ct. 492 (2022) (No. 22-5113), and for good reason. 
All circuits, including the court below, agree that district courts’ factual findings 
about matters like the defendant’s dangerousness and flight risk are reviewed with 
deference, and there appears to be a general consensus that pure legal questions are 
reviewed de novo. Particularly given the centrality of the deferentially reviewed factual findings, see 18 U.S.C. 3142(g), any disagreement in the courts of appeals is too 
narrow and abstract to warrant certiorari. Furthermore, even if the question presented in applicant’s petition warranted review, this case would be a poor vehicle for 
resolving it. The court of appeals’ decision to reverse the release order was correct 
regardless of the stated standard of review. And applicant’s challenge to his pretrial 
detention will be moot in January, when his trial is scheduled to take place. 
Applicant’s claim could well have become moot already, but he has voluntarily 
delayed his trial multiple times in an admitted (Appl. 32) effort to avoid mootness. 
Therefore, even if applicant could show a likelihood of certiorari and reversal, his 
strategic delay would preclude him from showing that the denial of a stay would inflict irreparable harm upon him. A pretrial detainee’s self-prolonged detention is not 
a form of irreparable harm that is cognizable in equity, particularly when the de-

4 
tainee, like applicant, identifies no concrete way in which pretrial detention has hindered his preparation for trial. Finally, even if the stay calculus were close enough 
to require a weighing of the equities, the strong governmental and public interests in 
protecting the public and ensuring applicant’s appearance by detaining him pending 
trial would dwarf applicant’s interest in release. The application—as well as his alternative motion to expedite his petition for a writ of certiorari—should be denied. 
STATEMENT 
A. Pretrial Release Under The Bail Reform Act Of 1984 
Under the Bail Reform Act of 1984, Pub. L. No. 98-473, Tit. II, Ch. I, 98 Stat. 
1976, when a person is arrested for a federal crime, the judicial officer (typically a 
magistrate judge) “before whom [the] arrested person is brought shall order that such 
person be released or detained, pending judicial proceedings.” 18 U.S.C. 3141(a). The 
particulars of pretrial release or detention are governed by 18 U.S.C. 3142. Section 
3142(b) requires release on personal recognizance or bond “unless the judicial officer 
determines that such release will not reasonably assure the appearance of the person 
as required or will endanger the safety of any other person or the community.” 18 
U.S.C. 3142(b). In the latter event, the judicial officer may order the person released 
subject to conditions (e.g., “remain[ing] in the custody of a designated person,” “maintain[ing] employment”) that “will reasonably assure the appearance of the person as 
required and the safety of any other person and the community.” 18 U.S.C. 
3142(c)(1)(B). 
But “[i]f, after a hearing * * * , the judicial officer finds that no condition or 
combination of conditions will reasonably assure the appearance of the person as required and the safety of any other person and the community, such judicial officer 
shall order the detention of the person before trial.” 18 U.S.C. 3142(e)(1); see 18

5 
U.S.C. 3142(f) (“The facts the judicial officer uses to support a finding pursuant to 
subsection (e) that no condition or combination of conditions will reasonably assure 
the safety of any other person and the community shall be supported by clear and 
convincing evidence.”). In undertaking that inquiry, the judicial officer is required to 
consider “the available information concerning— 
(1) the nature and circumstances of the offense charged, including whether 
the offense is a crime of violence, a violation of [18 U.S.C.] 1591, a Federal 
crime of terrorism, or involves a minor victim or a controlled substance, firearm, explosive, or destructive device; 
(2) the weight of the evidence against the person; 
(3) the history and characteristics of the person, including— 
(A) the person’s character, physical and mental condition, family 
ties, employment, financial resources, length of residence in the community, community ties, past conduct, history relating to drug or alcohol 
abuse, criminal history, and record concerning appearance at court proceedings; and 
(B) whether, at the time of the current offense or arrest, the person 
was on probation, on parole, or on other release pending trial, sentencing, appeal, or completion of sentence for an offense under Federal, 
State, or local law; and 
(4) the nature and seriousness of the danger to any person or the community that would be posed by the person’s release. 
18 U.S.C. 3142(g). 
A defendant who is ordered detained pending trial is “committed to the custody 
of the Attorney General for confinement in a corrections facility separate, to the extent practicable, from persons awaiting or serving sentences or being held in custody 
pending appeal,” and he must “be afforded reasonable opportunity for private consultation with counsel.” 18 U.S.C. 3142(i)(2) and (3). A magistrate judge’s order granting release or ordering detention under the Bail Reform Act is subject to review by 
the district court and then appeal to the court of appeals, by either the government 
or the defendant. See 18 U.S.C. 3145(c); United States v. Delker, 757 F.2d 1390, 1393

6 
(3d Cir. 1985) (“[E]ither party is entitled to prompt appellate review of the order of 
the district court.”). 
B. Factual Background 
Applicant “is a self-professed member of Antifa—short for anti-fascist—based 
in Minneapolis, Minnesota.” Pet. App. 3a (footnote omitted). He “has stated that he’s 
willing to die in what ‘he views as’ an ‘ideological battle’ against ‘violent fascist government actions and [their] supporters.’” Ibid. (brackets and citation omitted). He 
“has failed to appear for state criminal proceedings multiple times, was once ‘listed 
as an absconder’ by a state court, and had an active warrant for his arrest in Iowa” 
at the time this case arose. Id. at 22a (brackets and citation omitted); see id. at 52a53a (Bloomekatz, J., dissenting). 
“Around January 2026, [applicant] undertook a series of escalating steps to 
oppose Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s actions in Minneapolis and broadcast his efforts to a social-media following.” Pet. App. 3a. “As the month progressed, 
[applicant’s] social-media posts transitioned into direct calls for violence against federal agents and their supporters.” Ibid. For example, he “proclaimed that the situation in Minneapolis was ‘kill or be killed’”; “encouraged his online followers to ‘hunt’ 
ICE by ‘sacrificing’ their ‘vehicles’”; “urged his followers to ‘f**king fight’ ICE and ‘put 
hands’ on law-enforcement agents and ‘take their f**king guns’”; “suggested that he 
and his followers should ‘have a little f**king fun’ by ‘identifying every single’ ICE 
agent, ‘at the barrel of a gun’ if necessary”; “lamented that protestors had yet to 
‘march on f**king Whipple’—the federal building in Minneapolis—‘with guns’”; and 
stated “that he was ‘not talking about peaceful protests anymore’” and “that Minneapolis was ‘where ICE has come to die.’” Id. at 3a-4a (brackets and citations omitted). 
Applicant “specifically requested funds” from his social-media followers “to

7 
help him ‘evade’ detection by law enforcement,” and he received “between $10,000 
and $15,000.” Pet. App. 4a-5a (citation omitted). “After [applicant] posted calls for 
‘boots on the ground’ to a local intersection near ICE agents and urged his followers 
to ‘get your f**king guns and stop these f**king people,’ Instagram deleted [applicant’s] account.” Id. at 5a (brackets and citation omitted). “Yet he quickly resurfaced 
with a different account—employing the username ‘@antifa.kaos’—and a new series 
of online postings.” Ibid. (citation omitted). 
“On January 29, 2026, [applicant] allegedly ‘doxxed’ J.S., ‘a pro-ICE individual,’ by publishing” on social media “what he claimed was J.S.’s name, phone number, 
birth month and year, and address,” as well as “what he thought was the address and 
phone number of J.S.’s parents.” Pet. App. 5a-6a (citation omitted). Applicant “described J.S. as a ‘bb nazi boy’ and said ‘we can all knock on strangers doors . . . See 
you soon kiddo—stay safe out here.’” Id. at 6a (citation omitted). 
Two days before his eventual arrest, in a conversation on the messaging app 
Signal, applicant “pitched himself as able to assist in soliciting a murder.” Pet. App. 
15a; see id. at 14a. Another Signal user “allegedly contacted [applicant] with a request to help ‘kill’ a man named J.P., a former high-ranking government official.” Id.
at 5a (citation omitted). Applicant responded “in the chat that ‘we do stuff, me and 
my family of friends’ and ‘we like to know about people who deserve consequences,’” 
and “then asked for ‘credible verifiable information’ that he could pass onto his ‘team’ 
so it could ‘assess the situation.’” Ibid. (brackets and citations omitted). 
C. Procedural History 
The government charged applicant by complaint in the Eastern District of 
Michigan with one count of cyberstalking, in violation of 18 U.S.C. 2261A(2), and one 
count of transmitting interstate threats, in violation of 18 U.S.C. 875(c), both of which

8 
related to his conduct with respect to J.S. Pet. App. 6a-7a. “During his arrest, [applicant] allegedly began ‘pushing’ agents and ‘spitting on them’ while stating that he 
would ‘beat’ them,” and “also told the arresting agents ‘don’t let me out.’” Id. at 6a 
(brackets and citation omitted). “During his booking photo, [applicant] flashed two 
middle fingers at the camera” and said, “‘This is for the judge.’” Ibid. (citation omitted). 
1. “Following a detention hearing, a magistrate judge in Minnesota ordered [applicant] detained pretrial under the Bail Reform Act.” Pet. App. 6a. The 
magistrate judge found “that [applicant] was ‘a danger to the community’ given his 
‘implied threat to injure, harass or intimidate J.S. and his parents’ and his ‘voluminous’ social-media posts ‘encouraging his supporters to join him in obstructing, impeding, and assaulting officers.’” Ibid. (brackets and citation omitted). The magistrate judge also cited applicant’s “‘lack of job security,’ ‘admitted lack of stable housing,’ and expressed ‘desire to “evade” law enforcement,’” which “rendered him a flight 
risk.” Ibid. (citation omitted). 
Applicant was transferred to the Eastern District of Michigan, where a grand 
jury indicted him for cyberstalking and interstate transmission of threats. Pet. App. 
7a. He appealed the magistrate judge’s detention order to the district court, which 
held a hearing and then revoked the detention order. Ibid. The court acknowledged 
the “very serious” nature of “[c]yberstalking and threats on the internet,” associating 
that conduct with both “bullying * * * among little and high school students” and 
“people actually using it to be involved with serious crimes, including up to physically 
harming people in Federal Court.” Id. at 145a. And the court recognized that “the 
Government made a very strong argument that there was some protection of the public involved.” Id. at 143a. “[U]nfortunately,” the court continued, “in our nation at

9 
this time, I think people are viewing the protection of the public kind of like a twoway street. It depends on what side of the street you’re on whether or not an individual might feel they are protected or in need of protection.” Ibid. And it stated that it 
had “looked at the entire case in regard to whether or not I could address that with 
conditions that might protect everyone.” Ibid.
The district court ordered applicant to be released “to his mother’s home in 
Minnesota subject to a series of conditions,” including that he “submit to GPS monitoring”; “‘refrain from posting on social media’”; “forgo accessing the internet with 
anything other than two approved devices (one phone and one computer)”; “‘not engage in assaultive, threatening, or harassing behavior or statements’”; and remain at 
home “except for employment; education; religious services; medical, substance use 
or mental health treatment; attorney visits; court appearances; court-ordered obligations; or essential activities approved in advance by the court or pretrial services office or supervising officer.” Pet. App. 7a, 71a (brackets and citation omitted). 
2. The government appealed the district court’s release order to the court 
of appeals and sought an emergency stay. Pet. App. 7a. A divided panel of the court 
of appeals granted the stay, ibid., and subsequently reversed the release order, id. at 
1a-64a.2
a. The court of appeals found that the Bail Reform Act “mandates [applicant’s] pretrial detention” because “the Government has met its burden of proving 
[his] dangerousness” and “no condition or combination of conditions will reasonably 
assure the safety of J.S. and the community.” Pet. App. 8a. As to the appellate stand2 After issuance of the stay, the government “obtained a second grand jury 
indictment against [applicant] in the District of Minnesota” charging him “and several others with conspiracy to impede or injure a federal officer, solicitation to commit 
a crime of violence, and transmitting interstate threats.” Pet. App. 7a-8a; see Indictment, United States v. Sant, No. 26-cr-115 (June 11, 2026).

10 
ard of review of a pretrial release order, the court stated “that ‘mixed questions of law 
and fact’ and ‘legal conclusions,’” and “‘the ‘ultimate question whether pretrial detention is warranted,’” are subject to “‘de novo consideration.’” Id. at 9a. The court made 
clear, however, that “the district court’s factual findings” are reviewed “for clear error.” Ibid. (citations omitted). The court then considered the district court’s assessment of the factors set forth in the Bail Reform Act: “the nature and circumstances 
of the offense charged,” “the weight of the evidence against the person,” “the nature 
and seriousness of the danger to any person or the community that would be posed 
by the person’s release,” and “the history and characteristics of the person.” 18 U.S.C. 
3142(g). 
First, the court of appeals observed that “[n]either [applicant] nor the dissent 
disputes that the charged offenses are serious.” Pet. App. 12a. The court described 
as “legally unsound” the suggestion “that the charged offenses could sweep in minor 
conduct like schoolyard ‘bullying.’” Id. at 13a (citation omitted). Second, the court 
observed that the weight of the evidence was strong, explaining that applicant’s numerous “threatening statements ‘weigh strongly in favor of dangerousness’” and rejecting applicant’s effort “to cast” those statements “as empty bravado” “[n]ow that 
[the] threats have come under legal scrutiny.” Id. at 14a, 17a (brackets and citation 
omitted). Third, the court observed that applicant’s release would pose a serious danger to the community in light of the “well-documented harms” of “Internet-based 
threats like those [applicant] is charged with making” and applicant’s “willingness to 
entertain targeted threats on specific individuals” like J.P. Id. at 19a. The court also 
explained that the “district court’s apparent attempt to draw equivalency between 
[applicant’s] threats and the actions of federal law enforcement” was legally erroneous because “[t]he Bail Reform Act focuses on the danger the defendant poses,” and

11 
“[t]he district court’s views on the Executive Branch’s immigration policy have no 
bearing on that inquiry.” Id. at 19a-20a. And fourth, the court acknowledged that 
applicant’s “history and characteristics” weighed “‘slightly against dangerousness,’ 
as [applicant] has no violent criminal history,” but observed that “the Government 
‘ha[d] met its burden’ of ‘proving dangerousness by clear and convincing evidence’” 
even without evidence of “a violent criminal history.” Id. at 20a (brackets and citation 
omitted). 
The court of appeals further agreed with the government that “no condition or 
combination of conditions” short of detention would “‘reasonably assure’ the safety of 
J.S. and the community.” Pet. App. 21a (citation omitted). The court observed that 
the district court’s “conditions of release mostly ‘hinge on’ [applicant’s] ‘good faith 
compliance,’” while applicant’s “actions around the time of his arrest” and “pattern of 
failing to appear for prior judicial proceedings” in the past “point[ed] toward ‘an unacceptably high risk that’ [he] will disregard the conditions.” Id. at 21a-22a (citations 
omitted). The court of appeals also observed that “the online nature of [applicant’s] 
conduct further diminishe[d] the effectiveness of the district court’s conditions of release,” because, among other things, the “release order, which authorizes [applicant] 
to leave home confinement for ‘employment,’ ‘education,’ and various other reasons, 
would provide [him] with ample opportunities to ‘access the internet’ via unmonitored 
devices.” Id. at 22a (citations omitted). 
b. Judge Bloomekatz dissented. Pet. App. 27a-64a. She agreed with the 
majority that “[t]he district court’s factual findings are reviewable only for clear error” and “its legal conclusions are reviewed de novo,” id. at 39a, and further stated 
that “the district court’s application of the facts to the pretrial detention standard” 
should be reviewed “with ‘due deference,’” id. at 43a (citation omitted). On the merits,

12 
Judge Bloomekatz viewed applicant’s conduct as less serious and less indicative of 
dangerousness than did the majority. See id. at 43a-58a. For example, she understood applicant’s statement about his followers identifying ICE agents “at the barrel 
of a gun” as referring to the followers’ being “threatened at the ‘barrel of a gun,’” id.
at 49a (citation omitted), and viewed applicant’s Signal exchange about murdering 
J.P. to weigh only “slightly in favor of a finding of dangerousness,” id. at 51a. Judge 
Bloomekatz also considered the district court’s conditions of release sufficient to ensure applicant’s appearance and to protect the community. Id. at 58a-64a. 
3. On September 18, 2026, 37 days after the court of appeals’ decision, applicant filed a petition for a writ of certiorari (No. 26-391). Nearly a week after that, 
on September 24, he filed a motion in the court of appeals to recall the court of appeals’ mandate and stay its judgment pending the disposition of the certiorari petition. Appl. App. 1a. Judge Hermandorfer—the author of the majority opinion, to 
whom the motion was referred under circuit procedure—denied the motion. Id. at 
1a-7a. In doing so, she highlighted applicant’s failure to “seek to justify his weekslong 
failure to seek any relief prior to the mandate’s issuance.” Id. at 3a-4a. And she 
observed that petitioner’s request for a stay did not “appear compelling on its own 
terms.” Id. at 4a. 
Judge Hermandorfer explained that while applicant’s “cert petition principally 
rests the case for Supreme Court intervention on the presence of a circuit split over 
which standard of review governs district courts’ detention decisions under the Bail 
Reform Act,” the asserted conflict was decades-old and not “as lopsided or stark as 
[applicant’s] petition contends.” Appl. App. 5a. She further rejected applicant’s depiction of “the standard of review as outcome determinative” in this case, and explained that the “core objection” of Judge Bloomekatz’s panel dissent “boil[ed] down

13 
to a factual disagreement that ‘does not implicate the circuit split’ asserted.” Id. at 
6a (quoting BP P.L.C. v. Mayor & City Council, 593 U.S. 230, 246 (2021)). 
In addition, Judge Hermandorfer noted “problems with [applicant’s] particular 
vehicle” for this Court’s review, including “the odds that his pretrial-detention claim 
will soon become moot” because “trial is currently set to begin in early November 
2026.” Appl. App. 3a, 6a. She also indicated that the balance of equities favored the 
government, since it “appears that [applicant] has offered to voluntarily extend his 
detention to insulate his petition from mootness” and “‘law enforcement and public 
safety interests’” weighed in favor of applicant’s detention pending trial. Id. at 6a 
(citation omitted). 
4. On September 29, 2026, the day after his request to recall the mandate 
was denied, applicant filed his application for a stay pending the disposition of his 
petition for a writ a certiorari, along with an alternative motion to expedite consideration of the petition, in this Court. The motion noted that “[t]he parties have stipulated to a further 60-day extension on th[e] start date” of applicant’s trial but that 
“[a]t the conclusion of that trial, the Sixth Circuit’s pretrial detention order will have 
run its course” and the pretrial detention issue will “become moot.” Mot. 3. Applicant 
therefore urged the Court to “grant certiorari and decide the question presented expeditiously, before the trial in [his] case concludes.” Ibid. On September 30, the 
district court granted the 60-day extension, scheduling applicant’s trial to begin on 
January 12, 2027. 
ARGUMENT 
The application for a stay should be denied. To obtain a stay pending the disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari, “an applicant must show (1) a reasonable 
probability that four Justices will consider the issue sufficiently meritorious to grant

14 
certiorari; (2) a fair prospect that a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the 
judgment below; and (3) a likelihood that irreparable harm will result from the denial 
of a stay.” Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam). In “close 
cases,” the Court will balance the equities and weigh the relative harms. Ibid. Applicant fails to make the requisite showings. 
I. APPLICANT IS UNLIKELY TO SUCCEED IN OBTAINING CERTIORARI 
AND REVERSAL OF THE JUDGMENT BELOW 
This Court is unlikely to grant applicant’s pending petition for certiorari, much 
less reverse the Sixth Circuit’s judgment. See Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190. Applicant contends that certiorari is warranted to resolve a decades-old disagreement 
in the courts of appeals about the appellate standard of review for detention decisions, 
but the asserted conflict is overstated and amorphous—indeed, this Court denied a 
petition for certiorari raising the same conflict in 2022. See Gray v. United States, 
143 S. Ct. 492 (2022) (No. 22-5113). Even if the posited conflict did warrant this 
Court’s intervention, this case would be a poor vehicle for resolving the question presented. 
A. The Asserted Circuit Conflict Does Not Warrant This Court’s Review 
Applicant’s certiorari petition (at i) presents the question “[w]hether an appellate court should review a district court’s order granting or denying pretrial release 
de novo * * * or whether the appellate court owes some deference to the district 
court’s determination.” He contends (Appl. 14-20) that this Court should grant review to resolve a three-way conflict among the circuits on that question. In his view, 
the Sixth, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits “review pretrial detention orders de novo,” Appl. 14; see Appl. 14-16 (citing, e.g., Pet. App. 9a; United States v. 
Hazime, 762 F.2d 34, 37 (6th Cir. 1985); United States v. Cook, 87 F.4th 920, 921 (8th

15 
Cir. 2023); United States v. Santos-Flores, 794 F.3d 1088, 1090 (9th Cir. 2015); United 
States v. Cisneros, 328 F.3d 610, 613, 616 (10th Cir. 2003); United States v. Hurtado, 
779 F.2d 1467, 1470, 1471-1472 (11th Cir. 1985)); the Second, Fourth, Fifth, and D.C. 
Circuits review “for clear error or abuse of discretion,” Appl. 16; see Appl. 17-19 (citing, e.g., United States v. Zhang, 55 F.4th 141, 146 (2d Cir. 2022); United States v. 
Vane, 117 F.4th 244, 249 (4th Cir. 2024); United States v. Flores, 53 F.4th 313, 315 
(5th Cir. 2022) (per curiam); United States v. Vasquez-Benitez, 919 F.3d 546, 551 (D.C. 
Cir. 2019)); and the First, Third, and Seventh Circuits “conduct[] independent review 
of the detention decision but temper[] that review with deference to the district court’s 
firsthand assessment of the defendant and the case,” Appl. 19; see Appl. 19-21 (citing, 
e.g., United States v. Tortora, 922 F.2d 880, 882 (1st Cir. 1990); United States v. 
Delker, 757 F.2d 1390, 1400 (3d Cir. 1985); United States v. Portes, 786 F.2d 758, 763 
(7th Cir. 1986)). But applicant significantly overstates the scope of any disagreement 
among the courts of appeals. 
As a threshold matter, “[a]ll circuits”—not just the ones that applicant describes as the most deferential ones—“afford some deference to the district court’s 
factual determinations in ruling on pretrial release.” Br. in Opp. at 11, Gray, supra
(No. 22-5113) (Gray Opp.) (citing cases).3 In particular, all five of the circuits—including the court below—that applicant characterizes as applying a de novo standard 
(Appl. 14-16) review district courts’ factual findings in this context for clear error. 
See Pet. App. 9a; Cook, 87 F.4th at 921; Santos-Flores, 794 F.3d at 1090; Cisneros, 
328 F.3d at 613; Hurtado, 779 F.2d at 1472. The three circuits that applicant describes as conducting an “independent review” “tempered by a degree of deference,” 
3 The government has served applicant with a copy of its brief in opposition in 
Gray, which is also available on this Court’s electronic docket.

16 
Appl. 19 (citation omitted), are likewise deferential to the district court’s determination of the facts. See United States v. O’Brien, 895 F.2d 810, 813-814 (1st Cir. 1990); 
United States v. Suppa, 799 F.2d 115, 120 (3d Cir. 1986); Portes, 786 F.2d at 762. 
Thus, “[w]hile the characterization of the standard” of review among those eight circuits “is somewhat different,” “in practice the scope of review is the same under either 
approach.” Hurtado, 779 F.2d at 1471; accord O’Brien, 895 F.2d at 813 (“[T]he two 
independent standards are roughly equivalent, despite their apparent differences”). 
And because the legal assessment of the factors listed in the statute proceeds from 
“the available information,” 18 U.S.C. 3142(g), the universal practice of deference to 
a district court’s factual findings will minimize any actual differences in circuits’ approaches. 
Any differences are further minimized by what appears to be general agreement that pure legal questions are reviewed de novo. See, e.g., Vane, 117 F.4th at 
249 (reviewing a “question of statutory interpretation de novo”); United States v. 
Moreno, 857 F.3d 723, 725-726 (5th Cir. 2017) (“Absent an error of law, we review a 
pretrial detention order under ‘a deferential standard of review that we equate to the 
abuse-of-discretion standard.’”) (emphasis added; citation omitted); United States v. 
Abuhamra, 389 F.3d 309, 317 (2d Cir. 2004) (reviewing a “legal question de novo”).4 
In the Second Circuit, for instance, even the “district court’s ‘ultimate finding may be 
subject to plenary review if it rests on a predicate finding which reflects a misperception of a legal rule applicable to the particular factor involved.’” Zhang, 55 F.4th at 
146 (quoting United States v. Shakur, 817 F.2d 189, 197 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 484 
4 The D.C. Circuit appears not to have directly addressed the standard of review for legal aspects of a bail decision. See, e.g., United States v. Munchel, 991 F.3d 
1273, 1282 (2021) (reviewing “the District Court’s dangerousness determinations for 
clear error”); United States v. Hale-Cusanelli, 3 F.4th 449, 454-455 (2021) (similar, 
and citing Second Circuit precedent with approval).

17 
U.S. 840 (1987)). Accordingly, issues of, for example, what the statutory framework 
means would likely be reviewed in a similar fashion, notwithstanding the more general language that a court might use to describe its overall approach. And because 
similar (deferential) review of the facts and similar (de novo) review of the law are 
likely to create significant practical alignment in those overall approaches, “[t]he 
scope of any disagreement” among the courts of appeals on the standard of review for 
bail decisions “is narrow and unlikely to make a difference in a significant number of 
cases.” Gray Opp. at 11. 
Applicant identifies no cases involving similar bail determinations in which 
the appellate standard of review yielded different results on similar facts. That is 
likely why the asserted circuit conflict, which applicant describes (Appl. 24) as having 
arisen “decades ago,” has never warranted this Court’s intervention to date. Indeed, 
the government—which is a party to all Bail Reform Act proceedings and would have 
a strong interest in the standard of review for bail decisions if variations in the circuits’ approaches were consequential—has opposed review of that issue. See Gray 
Opp. at 7-12. And if there were any meaningful variation in circuit approaches, it 
would not work to the uniform advantage of either the government or defendants, as 
either could be the appellant or the appellee in an appeal from an order concerning 
pretrial detention. The Court has never granted certiorari on the issue, and applicant 
cannot show that it is likely to do so here. 
B. This Case Is An Unsuitable Vehicle For Resolving The Question Presented 
This case is an unlikely candidate for this Court’s review, let alone reversal, 
for additional reasons. 
1. The court of appeals’ decision is correct irrespective of the standard of

18 
review. As explained above, the Bail Reform Act requires detention pending trial if 
“no condition or combination of conditions will reasonably assure the appearance of 
the person as required and the safety of any other person and the community,” an 
inquiry that requires consideration of “the nature and circumstances of the offense 
charged,” “the weight of the evidence against the person,” “the history and characteristics of the person,” and “the nature and seriousness of the danger to any person or 
the community that would be posed by the person’s release.” 18 U.S.C. 3142(e)(1) 
and (g)(1)-(4). Based on those factors, the detention question here was not a close 
call. 
A grand jury indicted applicant for cyberstalking and threat offenses that are 
undisputedly “serious.” Pet. App. 12a. The factual particulars of his conduct are 
disturbing and highly suggestive of danger to others and the community: in addition 
to doxxing J.S., applicant made numerous public statements urging his followers on 
social media to commit violence against ICE agents and “‘march on’ a federal building 
‘with guns,’” and, among other things, “pitched himself as able to assist in soliciting 
a murder” of a former high-ranking government official. Id. at 15a, 17a (citation 
omitted); see id. at 13a. The district court appeared to “attempt to draw equivalency 
between [applicant’s] threats and the actions of federal law enforcement.” Id. at 19a; 
see id. at 143a. And the court granted conditions of release that would allow applicant to use the Internet—the means by which he carried out the charged offenses—
and easily evade the stated limitations on such use. See id. at 71a, 74a-75a (conditions of release allowing applicant to use the Internet, subject to monitoring, and 
leave his residence for a litany of purposes). Experience shows that applicant is not 
easily deterred: when Instagram deleted his account based on his online activity, he 
promptly created a new one and resumed the same activity. See id. at 5a.

19 
Furthermore, although the court of appeals had no need to reach the issue in 
light of applicant’s dangerousness, Pet. App. 11a, applicant would also present a serious risk of flight or failure to appear if released. In the period leading up to his 
commission of the charged offenses, applicant “specifically requested funds [from his 
followers] to help him ‘evade’ detection by law enforcement,” “provid[ing] the name of 
several financial-payment accounts for use in transferring him money” and ultimately receiving “between $10,000 and $15,000.” Id. at 4a-5a (citation omitted). 
Moreover, as the court of appeals noted, applicant “has failed to appear for state criminal proceedings multiple times, was once ‘listed as an absconder’ by a state court, 
and had an active warrant for his arrest in Iowa” at the time this case arose. Id. at 
22a (brackets and citation omitted); see id. at 52a-53a (Bloomekatz, J., dissenting). 
His aggressive conduct during his arrest and booking, id. at 6a, further exhibited a 
marked disrespect for law enforcement and the judiciary. 
Thus, as Judge Hermandorfer noted in denying applicant’s stay motion below, 
the appellate standard of review was not “outcome determinative” in this case. Appl. 
App. 6a. Indeed, this is not a case in which the district court’s participation in the 
bail hearing is likely to have given it much, if any, special insight: the evidence about 
the need to detain applicant pending trial consisted largely of applicant’s public conduct and statements, which were just as readily available to the court of appeals as 
they were to the district court. Contrary to applicant’s contention, the court of appeals did not simply “re-weigh[] the evidence itself, giving no deference to the district 
court’s situational awareness.” Appl. 23; see Appl. 25. The court instead explained 
that it was reviewing the facts under a highly deferential clear-error standard, Pet. 
App. 9a; indeed, the dissent did not meaningfully dispute the majority’s understanding of the facts. See, e.g., id. at 51a (“It is true that [applicant] responded to the

20 
[Signal] messages [about killing J.P.] by requesting ‘credible verifiable information’ 
that he could send to his team.”); id. at 52a-53a (acknowledging applicant’s previous 
failures to appear for criminal proceedings); id. at 53a (noting applicant’s fundraising 
to evade law enforcement but characterizing it as “bravado and social media posturing”). And the court criticized certain aspects of the district court’s reasoning as “legally unsound,” id. at 13a (emphasis added), or involving legally irrelevant “views on 
the Executive Branch’s immigration policy,” id. at 20a. 
Accordingly, even if this Court were to grant certiorari and reverse on the 
ground that the court of appeals applied an insufficiently deferential standard of review to the district court’s release order, the end result would likely be the same: 
applicant’s detention. This Court does not typically grant a writ of certiorari to “decide abstract questions of law * * * which, if decided either way, affect no right” of 
the parties. Supervisors v. Stanley, 105 U.S. 305, 311 (1882). Much less should it 
grant a stay under such circumstances. 
2. Applicant’s case is also a poor vehicle for this Court’s review because it 
“will soon become moot.” Appl. App. 6a. As applicant explains (Appl. 4), “[p]retrial 
detention orders expire,” and appeals challenging such orders become moot under 
Article III, “when trial ends.” See Murphy v. Hunt, 455 U.S. 478, 481 (1982) (per 
curiam) (observing a “claim to pretrial bail [is] moot once [the defendant is] convicted”); cf. Pet. App. 40a (Bloomekatz, J., dissenting) (noting that appellate courts 
“seldom see” “pretrial detention issues”). Applicant’s pretrial detention will end at 
the conclusion of his trial, which is scheduled to begin on January 12 and expected to 
last (by the government’s estimate) only two to three days. See Gray Opp. at 14 (noting that the petitioner’s pretrial-detention claim would likely “be moot before any 
decision on the merits is possible”).

21 
The imminency of trial would require this Court to grant applicant’s petition 
for certiorari, receive briefing, hold oral argument, and issue a decision all within 
approximately three months. See Appl. 5 (“request[ing] that the Court construe this 
stay application as a petition for certiorari, grant the stay application and certiorari, 
issue an expedited briefing schedule, and schedule the case for argument at the earliest opportunity”). That would be an exceptionally compressed schedule on which to 
decide any case, and an excessive strain to decide an issue that, as discussed above, 
is abstract and of little apparent practical importance. Applicant’s suggestion (Appl. 
5; Mot. 3-4) that the Court proceeded similarly in Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418 (2009), 
is incorrect. In Nken, the Court was able to take almost six months (from the petitioner’s filing of his stay application) to the issuance of its merits decision. See id. at 
423. Unlike Nken, in which a stay of removal was itself enough to pause all of the 
relevant proceedings, a stay of pretrial detention here would do nothing to prevent 
his forthcoming trial from mooting the pretrial-detention issue. In addition, even if 
the Court took applicant’s proposed path and reversed the decision below, its typical 
course would be to remand for application of the “correct standard” of review in the 
first instance, Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 257 (1986); see Nken, 
556 U.S. at 436, by which point applicant’s challenge to his pretrial detention would 
even more likely be moot. 
Applicant fails to explain why, if the appellate standard of review for bail decisions truly warranted this Court’s review, a case involving bail pending appeal—
which would lack the exigency of a case involving bail pending trial, where speedytrial concerns limit the duration of detention, see Appl. 22—would not be a more appropriate vehicle. Release or detention of a defendant pending appeal is governed by 
18 U.S.C. 3143, and a decision on bail pending appeal is appealable, like a decision

22 
on pretrial bail, under 18 U.S.C. 3145. See Hurtado, 779 F.2d at 1473 (“[T]he 1984 
Act makes no distinction between pre- and post-conviction review of denial of bail”). 
Although that posttrial context differs from the pretrial context in that detention becomes the default, the inquiry in both contexts involves many of the same considerations. See, e.g., 18 U.S.C. 3143(b)(A) (requiring detention pending appeal unless, inter alia, there is “clear and convincing evidence that the person is not likely to flee or 
pose a danger to the safety of any other person or the community if released”). And 
courts appear to describe the standards of review for each in similar terms. Compare, 
e.g., United States v. Garcia, 340 F.3d 1013, 1015 (9th Cir. 2003), and United States
v. Shoffner, 791 F.2d 586, 590 (7th Cir. 1986) (per curiam), with, respectively, SantosFlores, 794 F.3d at 1090, and Portes, 786 F.2d at 762-763.
II. THE BALANCE OF THE EQUITIES STRONGLY FAVORS THE GOVERNMENT 
Even beyond applicant’s inability to show a likelihood of certiorari and relief, 
the additional stay factors likewise do not support the emergency relief that he requests. 
As a threshold matter, applicant cannot establish that he faces irreparable 
harm warranting a stay. See Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190. Applicant appears to 
acknowledge that he has voluntarily delayed his trial date—and thereby voluntarily 
prolonged his own pretrial detention—“from April, to July, to September, to November,” and now to January, all to delay the pretrial-detention issue’s becoming moot 
with the conclusion of his trial. Appl. App. 6a; see Appl. 32 (representing that applicant “is willing to delay his trial in order to provide this Court an opportunity to resolve his petition for certiorari”). As Judge Hermandorfer noted in denying applicant’s stay motion below, such a “‘self-inflicted,’ strategic extension of detention”

23 
should not be deemed irreparable harm for purposes of obtaining equitable relief. 
Appl. App. 6a (quoting Second City Music, Inc. v. City of Chicago, 333 F.3d 846, 850 
(7th Cir. 2003)); accord Bennett v. Isagenix Int’l LLC, 118 F.4th 1120, 1129-1130 (9th 
Cir. 2024); 11A Charles Alan Wright et al., Federal Practice and Procedure § 2948.1 
(3d ed. 2013). Applicant has been dilatory in other respects as well, having waited 
more than six weeks after the Sixth Circuit’s decision and allowing its mandate to 
issue before seeking stays from that court and this one. See pp. 12-13, supra. 
Although applicant suggests (Appl. 32) that he needs pretrial release in order 
to adequately defend himself at trial, he describes no concrete ways in which his detention has prevented or impeded him from consulting with his counsel or otherwise 
preparing for trial. Rather, he offers only the general statement “that detained defendants are ‘hindered in their ability’ to ‘prepare their defense,’” quoting a 1972 decision of this Court involving a state prisoner, ibid. (quoting Barker v. Wingo, 407 
U.S. 514, 533) (brackets omitted), and ignoring the subsequently enacted Bail Reform 
Act’s guarantee of federally detained defendants’ access to “private consultation with 
counsel,” 18 U.S.C. 3142(i)(3). It is quite common for a federal defendant to be placed 
in pretrial custody, receive assistance of counsel there, and be given a fair public trial, 
all without being released. Applicant presents no reason why the same cannot be 
true for him. To the contrary, particularly given that the evidence concerns public 
online activity, and that applicant’s trial will last (by the government’s estimate) only 
two to three days, it is exceedingly unlikely that applicant’s detention has prevented 
or will prevent him from sufficiently preparing for his trial. 
In addition to the absence of imminent harm, the government’s and the public’s 
interests strongly support applicant’s continued detention pending his trial and outweigh applicant’s interest in release. See Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190. The gov-

24 
ernment has a compelling interest in protecting the public from individuals who engage in the criminal conduct with which applicant is charged. “Stalking can be devastating and dangerous”: “[h]arassers can hide behind online anonymity while tormenting others,” “[l]ives can be ruined, and in the most tragic instances, lives are 
lost.” Counterman v. Colorado, 600 U.S. 66, 89 (2023) (Sotomayor, J., concurring in 
part and concurring in the judgment). “Even isolated threatening speech can do real 
harm” by “disrupt[ing] lives” and “silenc[ing] the speech of others who become afraid 
to speak out.” Ibid. And “the internet has * * * made stalking and harassment even 
easier,” ibid., as applicant has shown. Such conduct is particularly pernicious when, 
as here, it involves law enforcement or members of the public who have or are perceived as having particular political views or associations. Cf. Doe v. Reed, 561 U.S. 
186, 242-243 (2010) (Thomas, J., dissenting) (noting the ease of threatening or harassing referendum signees). 
Here, applicant has called for violence against federal agents and property; 
doxxed and threatened someone based on the person’s “pro-ICE” views, leading to his 
indictment for violating federal cyberstalking and threat laws; entertained a proposal 
to murder a former government official; aggressively resisted arrest; and expressed 
disdain for judicial authority. His separate indictment in the District of Minnesota 
for additional serious offenses (including conspiring to impede or injure a federal officer), see note 2, supra, reinforces his likely danger to the community. Applicant has 
also solicited money for the purpose of evading law enforcement and has a history of 
not appearing for judicial proceedings. Yet the district court ordered applicant’s release subject to conditions that would permit him to leave his residence for numerous 
reasons and would enable him easily to access the Internet in unmonitored ways. 
Applicant’s release pending trial would pose unacceptably high risks to law

25 
enforcement and the public. Particularly compared with the limited supposed harms 
of applicant’s pretrial detention, the governmental and public interest in his continued detention—like the other stay factors—weigh strongly against this Court’s issuance of a stay. This Court should not grant one. 
CONCLUSION 
The application should be denied.
